units.title: Sanandajī's invocation
units.arabic_anchors: «بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم» · «الحمد من هدانا إلى طريق الإسلام» · «تهذيب الكلام وتقريب المرام».
units.english: In the name of God, the All-Merciful, the Compassionate. Praise to the One who guided us to the way of Islam; thanks to the One who granted us success in refining theological discourse and bringing its aims nearer. Blessings and peace upon Muḥammad, the master and messenger sent to mankind, and upon his family. The praise is cast in deliberately rhythmic prose; its invocation continues on the next leaf.
units.proof_note: Retained upper first-pass rendering, newly source-position checked; exact rhymed epithets not all separately translated.

units.title: Distinct secondary invocation, linked to Wasīm I:3
units.arabic_anchors: «بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم» · «الحمد لله الذي هدانا لدين الإسلام» · «وفقنا على تحرير المقاصد الدينية».
units.english: A **separate** invocation begins in the lower print: praise to God for guidance to Islam and assistance in elucidating religious purposes, with blessings upon Muḥammad and his family. The writer names himself in the following leaf as **Muḥammad al-Wasīm**. This is not the tail of Sanandajī's upper invocation.
units.proof_note: Established authorial-preface stream, *retained* from the prior English translation. Exact full preface in the linked Stage51 source, not reproduced as an independent new translation here.

units.title: Sanandajī explains his undertaking
units.arabic_anchors: «فيقول العبد الفقير إلى ألطاف ربه» · «عبد القادر» · «قسم التهذيب من الكلام» · «العلامة الثاني السعد التفتازاني».
units.english: Sanandajī identifies himself as ʿAbd al-Qādir, a servant dependent upon God's favour, and describes the kalām section of Taftāzānī's *Tahdhīb* as unusually concise, carefully ordered and rich in subtle points. Although pressed by circumstances, he was urged by a person whose request he could not disregard to explain this difficult text. He therefore undertook a commentary intended to clarify its expressions and recover its intended senses. The sentence continues on I:4.
units.proof_note: Inherited source-reading of the sharḥ author's preface; ornamental rhetoric not yet independently proofed word by word.

units.title: Wasīm names himself and describes the commentary's origin
units.arabic_anchors: «محمد الوسيم ابن المرحوم الشيخ محمد سعيد» · «ومنهم الأخ الأكبر الماهر الشيخ عبد القادر» · «يراجع شرح المقاصد».
units.english: In the lower stream, Muḥammad al-Wasīm explicitly names himself. He explains that students studying Taftāzānī with their father included his elder brother ʿAbd al-Qādir. During that study, ʿAbd al-Qādir consulted *Sharḥ al-Maqāṣid*, recording subtle explanations in brief marginal notes; he later made those into a continuous commentary. The shared family and teaching setting explains why the page must preserve **two different narrating voices**.
units.proof_note: Retained and positively attributed historical preface; exact previous Arabic–English draft available in the Stage51 module. A revised definitive English must be checked against the printed leaf, not merely that module.

units.title: Sanandajī's purpose and self-assessment
units.arabic_anchors: «معانيه وتوضيح عباراته» · «فجاء بحمد الله ذلك شرحاً» · «خالياً عن شوائب الخلل والنقصان» · «فانظر ثم ارجع البصر هل ترى من فطور».
units.english: The commentary aims to elucidate obscure expressions, clarify intellectual difficulties, and make subtle points accessible. The writer expresses the hope that his labour will be free of significant defects, yet rhetorically invites inspection: ‘Return your gaze: do you see any fissures?’ His praise also acknowledges the teaching of his father and the circumstances that allowed the work to come into being. This is an **authorial rhetorical appeal**, not a modern editorial claim of textual perfection.
units.proof_note: Existing main-preface translation retained, with the scriptural-sounding allusion preserved as such.

units.title: Revisions, hardship and relocation
units.arabic_anchors: «الشرح مرة ثانية» · «جرح وتعديل» · «أكتب على الشرح حواشي» · «تموجت أمواج المحن والفتن».
units.english: Wasīm recounts that his elder brother revised the commentary, changing or clarifying some passages. He had long hoped to compose notes on the commentary, to resolve difficult locations and questions. Repeated events delayed him, and disturbances grew until his elder brother left his homeland. Wasīm's account includes the brother's reception in Sulaymāniyya and Wasīm's own grief at separation. It is autobiographical source material; **these historical particulars are not part of Sanandajī's original kalām argument**.
units.proof_note: Positively identified Wasīm text, prior translation preserved separately. Exact literary lineation and poetry require final source proof.

units.title: The title *Taqrīb al-Marām*
units.arabic_anchors: «سميته تقريب المرام في شرح تهذيب الكلام» · «محمد الهاشمي القرشي».
units.english: Having composed the commentary, Sanandajī gives it the title *Taqrīb al-Marām fī Sharḥ Tahdhīb al-Kalām*—roughly ‘Bringing the Intended Aim Near: a Commentary on the Refinement of Theological Discourse.’ He closes with a prayer that it benefit its readers and a benediction upon Muḥammad the Hāshimī and Qurashī. The prayer, like the opening, is in rhymed prose.
units.proof_note: Inherited upper translation, not an entirely newly certified diplomatic rendering.

units.title: Wasīm closes his introduction
units.arabic_anchors: «سنة ألف ومائتين وثلاثة وسبعين» · «النبوة».
units.english: Wasīm's prefatory account concludes with its own reflection on the work's publication, the benefits and difficulties of the commentary, and a stated completion date of **1273 AH**. That date belongs to **his account of completing the prefatory/annotation work**, not automatically to the Būlāq edition or to every portion of the sharḥ. Its exact referent should be established from the entire closing sentence during independent checking.
units.proof_note: Retained source-attributed Wasīm text. Do not add 4 new 'complete translated pages' to this stage by repackaging an earlier translation.

units.title: Can the chapter plan itself count as the beginning of kalām?
units.arabic_anchors: «(قوله هذا قسم الكلام من التهذيب)» · «غاية تهذيب الكلام» · «في تحرير المنطق وتحرير الكلام» · «ألفاظ ... قسماً من العلم».
units.english: The marginal writer examines what is implied by calling this the kalām division of a book which also concerns logic. One might take the wording to mean that the book is ‘refined’ in its entirety; another reading limits the title's effect to the matters explicitly treated under it. The gloss distinguishes a **textual division**, a **field of knowledge**, and the act of **refining a discourse** about that field. The point is relevant because the two sections need not have precisely the same objects, terminology, or demonstrative aim.
units.proof_note: Source-facing marginal reading; not every subordinate example individually translated.

units.title: Preliminary matters and subject-matter
units.arabic_anchors: «المقدمة» · «الحدّ والموضوع» · «مباحث العلم والنظر» · «التعريف».
units.english: The marginal argument also asks which preliminary matters are genuinely needed for the science. A definition of a discipline may address its name, subject, end and benefit; a preliminary discussion may also address the meaning of knowledge and the role of inquiry. Those questions are introduced as **instruments** for the ensuing theological investigation. The writer warns against treating every preliminary logical discussion as though it were already a doctrinal conclusion.
units.proof_note: Connected interpretative lower text, requires literal second pass.

units.title: On the expression ‘section of kalām’
units.arabic_anchors: «(قوله أي ما سيأتي عليك)» · «هذا إشارة من الألفاظ من حيث دلالتها على المعاني» · «(قوله المسمى بالتهذيب)».
units.english: On the words “what will come before you,” the commentator points out how the demonstrative is attached to what follows in the written exposition. The title ‘Tahdhīb’ and the expression ‘the division of kalām’ are accordingly explained as designating a **part of a composed text**, not an independently existing scientific object. The gloss also discusses the phrasing and attribution of the title; a short name in the final line is not confidently legible.
units.proof_note: Short ruled annotation with an uncertain proper-name reading.

units.title: The intended portion of the book
units.arabic_anchors: «(هذا) أي ما سيأتي عليك (قسم الكلام من) الكتاب المسمى (بالتهذيب)» · «وقع التبويب» · «المقدمة أولاً».
units.english: “This”—that is, the material about to be presented—is the **division on kalām** in the book called *al-Tahdhīb*. The reason the author has arranged it in chapters is that there are matters which ought to be introduced before the substantive questions of theology. They form the first chapter, a preliminary section; only once those conceptual preliminaries have been set out can the later questions be investigated. The work's division and naming are therefore not arbitrary ornaments but mark the progression of the inquiry.
units.proof_note: Upper text first-pass source-guided reading.

units.title: What does ‘chapter’ denote?
units.arabic_anchors: «في الباب الأول في المقدمة» · «الظاهر أن الأبواب هي الألفاظ أو النقوش» · «النظر أولاً».
units.english: The lower writer observes that a ‘chapter’ can designate the **written headings or sections** of the treatise rather than a metaphysical part of the subject-matter. He is concerned to avoid a purely verbal inference from a heading to a division of reality. The introductory chapter is not the whole of kalām merely because it contains prerequisites of kalām; its function is to explain what the science is and how its arguments proceed.
units.proof_note: Marginal source-facing explanation; some editorial connective phrasing used.

units.title: What should come before the scientific questions?
units.arabic_anchors: «مباحث العلم والنظر» · «التصور والتصديق» · «المقدمة» · «ما يتوقف عليه الشروع في مسائل العلم».
units.english: The gloss asks whether the actual investigation of first principles should precede the definition of the science, or whether the introductory description is sufficient for a reader who has not yet learned the relevant principles. Some knowledge of **conception**, **assent**, and **valid reasoning** is indispensable before proof is possible. But it does not follow that every such preliminary must itself be independently proven at the beginning of the treatise. The author is explaining a pedagogical order, not claiming that the order of printed headings dictates the order of things in the world.
units.proof_note: Provisional connected gloss; word-exhaustive proof pending.

units.title: The beginning of the introduction
units.arabic_anchors: «(الباب الأول في المقدمة)» · «تقدّمه معرفة حدّه وموضوعه وغايته».
units.english: “Chapter One: the Introduction.” Before undertaking the theological proofs, the reader is given an account of the science's **definition**, **subject**, and **aim**. These preparatory notions make the manner in which the subsequent problems are investigated intelligible.
units.proof_note: Title and middle short printed line; not a named authorial note.

units.title: Sequence of the later chapters
units.arabic_anchors: «الثلاثة في الوجود وهو الباب الثاني في الأمور العامة» · «الثالث في الأعراض» · «الرابع في الجواهر» · «الخامس ... بالواجب تعالى» · «السادس في السمعيات ... الباب الخامس في الإلهيات».
units.english: After the preliminary chapter, the subject is arranged in a progression: the **general matters of being**; matters concerning **accidents**; matters concerning **substances**; the **Necessary Existent**, or what pertains to God; and finally the **things known by transmission**, where the revealed reports and the mission of the Messenger are treated. The chapter headings have their own technical ordering, and the commentator explains how the labels for the wider theological divisions correspond to the actual sequence within the *Tahdhīb*.
units.proof_note: Upper source reading. Chapter numeration across the very abbreviated line should be rechecked before formal table of contents reconstruction.

units.title: Why distinguishing kalām by ‘belief’ is difficult
units.arabic_anchors: «(قوله خاصة)» · «الاختصاص بعلم الكلام» · «الاختصاص ... على ما صرح به المصنف في شرح المقاصد» · «اعتقاد القلب».
units.english: The marginal commentator insists that the difference between kalām and logic or law cannot simply be a difference in **subject terms**. Many theological proofs concern bodies, accidents, possibility, causality and language, all of which can also be examined in other disciplines. The relevant differentiation is through the **end for which the inquiry is undertaken**: establishing a religious belief rather than, for instance, deriving a legal action or analysing the formal structure of an inference.
units.proof_note: Lower source-guided analysis; not a complete literal transcription.

units.title: Necessary judgments and practical judgments
units.arabic_anchors: «الأحكام التي يتعلق الغرض بمجرد اعتقادها» · «وجوب القلب» · «الأحكام الشرعية» · «كيفية العمل».
units.english: Some religious judgments call for the **assent** of the believer; others are concerned with the manner of acting. The marginal writer examines whether this separation is absolute or is better expressed by a difference in the **proximate aim** of the relevant science. An obligatory practical act may also be something one must believe is obligatory; that does not make its detailed derivation a question of kalām. Likewise, a proposition about theological doctrine may have practical consequences without ceasing to be a doctrinal proposition.
units.proof_note: Connected lower reading, several compact examples unverified.

units.title: Remarks on the naming of the discipline
units.arabic_anchors: «(قال المصنف رحمه الله الكلام هو العلم الخ)» · «أي علم الكلام».
units.english: On the author's words “kalām is knowledge, etc.”: the phrase is intended as **‘the science of kalām’**, not a statement that every instance of speech counts as knowledge. The gloss alludes to other historical explanations of why the discipline came to be called ‘kalām’; these alternatives do not all supply its formal definition.
units.proof_note: Short ruled gloss, part source quotation and part source-facing clarification.

units.title: The specific scope of theological science
units.arabic_anchors: «الكلام خاصة» · «كمباحث العلم والنظر والدليل» · «لا تحصل العقائد بطريق النظر والاستدلال» · «الإلهيات خاصة».
units.english: The designation ‘kalām’ does not simply mean every investigation of **knowledge, inquiry, and evidence**. Those subjects also belong to logic and the theory of demonstration. Nor is its defining mark merely that doctrinal propositions are asserted. What distinguishes this science is the way its investigations are ordered toward establishing **religious convictions** through arguments. The statement therefore moves from the preparatory discussion to a definition of kalām.
units.proof_note: Upper text; one negative clause is printed compactly, so it is retained as a cautious interpretative rendering.

units.title: Definition through doctrinal knowledge
units.arabic_anchors: «(الكلام هو العلم بالعقائد)» · «وهي الأحكام التي يتعلق الغرض بمجرد اعتقادها بالقلب».
units.english: “Kalām is knowledge of the doctrines.” These are judgments for which the relevant end is **assent in the heart** as such, rather than the bodily execution of a practice. This distinction does not imply that religious practice is unimportant; rather, it determines the formal respect under which the science studies its judgments, in contrast to a discipline concerned with the practical derivation of rulings.
units.proof_note: Upper matn/sharḥ boundary read from printed punctuation.

units.title: Why the distinction does not reduce kalām to fiqh
units.arabic_anchors: «الفقه ذكرنا لا إجماع حيث يتعلق الغرض باعتقادها دون العمل بها» · «تدخل في التعريف» · «في أصول الفقه مقصودة لذاتها».
units.english: The marginal discussion distinguishes an act's being relevant to *belief about a ruling* from the act's *practical observance*. Some propositions examined in law or legal theory can enter theology under a different respect, namely when what matters is assent to a revealed judgment rather than deriving an action from it. That change of perspective does not turn kalām into jurisprudence: in legal theory, the principles are pursued for their role in establishing rulings; in kalām, a proposition can be discussed because of its relation to religious belief itself. The writer tests which disciplines would be improperly included if this regard were omitted from the definition.
units.proof_note: Lower-register source-facing explanation, several lines compressed in English.

units.title: The imitator, fallible assent and status of evidence
units.arabic_anchors: «(قوله عن الأدلة اليقينية)» · «(قوله سواء طابق الواقع أو لا)» · «(قوله أي المكتسب)».
units.english: On the phrase “from certain proofs,” the gloss presses the distinction between possession of a true belief and possession of it **through an argument**. The imitator may assent to a true theological proposition without himself knowing the proof. If every correct conviction were counted as the science of kalām, its boundary would expand beyond the intellectual activity under definition. Conversely, treating any proof the speaker calls “certain” as genuinely demonstrative risks admitting erroneous arguments. The author of the gloss does not allow the subjective impression of certainty to settle this issue.
units.proof_note: Argument summary grounded in visible anchors; literal clause mapping incomplete.

units.title: The intended scope of ‘acquired’
units.arabic_anchors: «(قوله أي المكتسب)» · «الدليل متعلق بالعلم» · «باعتبار تضمّنه معنى الاكتساب لا ...» · «الإذعان في المقاصد».
units.english: On “that is, acquired”: the phrase about proofs is understood as relating to knowledge **insofar as it is acquired**, rather than as an independent condition attached indiscriminately to every belief. This is a grammatical and conceptual clarification: it explains why the definition appeals to proofs where the activity of the discipline is demonstrative, without implying that every occurrence of the same theological proposition must be acquired by a proof.
units.proof_note: Short ruled gloss, provisional; final source reference requires verification.

units.title: Religious convictions rather than juridical practice
units.arabic_anchors: «الاعتقاد، أيضاً المقصود من العلم به علم الفقه» · «(الدينية) المنسوبة إلى دين نبينا محمد صلى الله عليه وعلى آله وسلم» · «سواء أكانت من الدين في الواقع ككلام أهل الحق أم لا ككلام الفرق المبتدعة».
units.english: What is at issue is **doctrinal assent**, not the objects of jurisprudential knowledge in their practical aspect. “Religious” means attributed to the religion of our Prophet Muḥammad—God bless him and his family and grant him peace. The designation can therefore include both propositions that truly belong to that religion, as the author understands the discourse of the orthodox, and propositions that are only **claimed** to belong to it, as in the discourse of groups he calls innovators. Such attribution does not imply that every proposition so named is correct. The author is defining the class of questions discussed in a discipline, not certifying every proposed answer.
units.proof_note: Upper source-facing, terms read from the scan; polemical labels belong to the historical text.

units.title: Evidence that yields certainty
units.arabic_anchors: «فإذا كان المراد من العلم مطلق التصديق سواء طابق الواقع أو لا ...» · «(عن الأدلة اليقينية) أي المكتسب».
units.english: If “knowledge” is interpreted indiscriminately as any assent, whether or not it corresponds to reality, the definition would also include mistaken conviction. The qualification “from **certain proofs**” is introduced to delimit the intended sort of acquired cognition. But it raises a further question: does certainty here qualify the *proof objectively*, the *knower's state*, or the *evidence as deemed certain by the proponent*? The next page examines these readings rather than presuming their equivalence.
units.proof_note: Upper passage close reading with terminal continuation to I:10.

units.title: Error, opinion and objective conformity
units.arabic_anchors: «(قوله العلم اليقيني)» · «المطابق للواقع في نفس الأمر» · «(قوله الدليل اليقيني)» · «لا يخرج إدراك المخطئ».
units.english: On “certain knowledge,” the gloss asks whether *conformity to reality* is built into the notion of knowledge. If it is, a wrong judgment cannot become knowledge merely through its firmness. If the proof is “certain” only **in the disputant's opinion**, incorrect judgments may again enter through that concession. A likely intended response distinguishes correctness from the psychological condition of firmness; both must be checked. The marginal writer is investigating the **scope of the definition**, not asserting that all reported opinions have the same evidential standing.
units.proof_note: Partial lower translation, no definitive transcription.

units.title: The difficult case of the imitator
units.arabic_anchors: «(قوله العقيدة بزعم المستدل)» · «المطابقة للواقع باعتقاده» · «التصديق الجازم سواء طابق الواقع أم لا» · «المقلد».
units.english: A person who imitates a teacher can hold a firm conviction and even, by good fortune, a true one; but that alone does not mean he possesses the **science** characterised by justified inference. The gloss tests whether the exclusion is achieved by “certain” or only by specifying the act of acquisition from proofs. It also distinguishes an opinion which is merely *probable*, a categorical **error**, and a firmly held **true** assertion. None should be conflated with the activity of establishing religious doctrines through arguments.
units.proof_note: Source-facing marginal account; lower proof remains open.

units.title: Does kalām concern only necessary propositions?
units.arabic_anchors: «اليقين ...» · «هل المراد ... القطعية» · «علم الكلام».
units.english: The discussion notes that a proof of a theological claim must not be judged conclusive merely because its proponent feels no doubt. Nor does the word *certainty* mean that every theological issue is a self-evident proposition. It concerns the character of the assent appropriately established by the investigation. The closing observation returns to the stated limits of the discipline and supplies the join to I:11.
units.proof_note: Condensed lower text; final compact sentences still need separate Arabic extraction.

units.title: Is certainty in the proof or in the mind?
units.arabic_anchors: «ذلك العلم عن أدلتها» · «العلم اليقيني» · «لأن الدليل اليقيني ما يفيد اليقين» · «المراد بالأدلة العقدية المعتقدة بزعم المستدل».
units.english: The qualification directs one to knowledge **through its proofs**, and the evidence called certain is, strictly speaking, that which gives rise to certainty. Yet a different reading is also reported: the proofs intended might be those **believed to be conclusive by the person arguing**. These are not equivalent. In one reading the definition selects genuinely warranted cognition; in the other it describes the kind of claim put forward by practitioners, including those who dispute one another.
units.proof_note: Upper text close reading; the narrow wording around *al-adilla al-ʿaqdiyya* is unclear and must be reviewed.

units.title: The boundaries of acquired religious knowledge
units.arabic_anchors: «ثم إنهم اعتبروا في أدلتها اليقين» · «لئلا عبرة بالظن في الاعتقادات» · «وعلم الرسول بالاعتقادات وكذا اعتقاد المقلد».
units.english: Because these are questions of faith, some authors demand certainty rather than mere probability. But the commentary asks about exceptional forms of correct theological assent: God's knowledge, prophetic knowledge, and the conviction of a person who merely follows another. The function of the word “science” in the definition must be **acquired and disciplined doctrinal knowledge**, not the simple occurrence of a true judgment in any knower whatever. The argument is continued on I:11.
units.proof_note: Upper text, joined I:10→11.

units.title: Whether imitation can count as justified knowledge
units.arabic_anchors: «(قوله وكذا اعتقاد المقلد)» · «أهل الكشف» · «المعتقد المقلد» · «الاعتقاد الجازم».
units.english: The lower author tests the previous claim about imitation. An imitator's conviction may be firmly held and correspond to reality, yet lack the evidence appropriate to a demonstrative science. In contrast, the settled cognition of a competent investigator may be acquired through the orderly pursuit of proof. The gloss distinguishes the issue **whether a belief is true** from the issue **whether its possessor can establish it**. That distinction bears directly on the definition of kalām by proofs.
units.proof_note: Lower argument partly interpretative.

units.title: Is ‘the known’ too broad a subject?
units.arabic_anchors: «(قوله موضوعه)» · «لفظ المعلوم» · «الموضوع عام» · «العقائد الدينية».
units.english: The subject term “the known” appears excessively broad, since it can include both what exists and what does not, and things studied by many other sciences. The commentator therefore insists on the delimiting **relation to religious doctrines**. Another question arises: does the word “known” refer to the *subject term* in every theorem, to all entities in the field, or to whatever is considered for the sake of proving theological conclusions? An adequate definition must not switch silently between these senses.
units.proof_note: Marginal source-facing reading; line-by-line correspondence pending.

units.title: Propositions versus constituent terms
units.arabic_anchors: «التصديق بوجود الموضوع» · «جزء من المعلوم» · «المبادئ التصورية» · «المبادئ التصديقية».
units.english: The margin elaborates the relation between knowing the *terms* of a proposition and assenting to the *proposition itself*. Demonstration presupposes conceptions of its terms, while the truth of a conclusion involves judgment. On that basis, subjects, predicates and first principles may all enter a discipline without each separately being the final object of its assent. This is relevant to whether the subject of kalām should be stated in terms of “the known” or in terms of the propositions it establishes.
units.proof_note: Provisional lower explanation, ending connects to I:12.

units.title: The Companions and the historical term ‘kalām’
units.arabic_anchors: «علم الصحابة» · «وإن لم يسمَّ في ذلك الزمان بالكلام» · «كما أن علمهم بالحساب ... لم يسمَّ به».
units.english: The knowledge possessed by the Prophet's Companions was not called “kalām” at the time, just as their knowledge of other matters was not necessarily named after the later disciplines in which those matters were organised. The historical **name** of a discipline does not determine whether earlier persons possessed the relevant knowledge. One must distinguish the activity or insight from the subsequent technical label applied to it.
units.proof_note: Upper short passage read from scan.

units.title: Subject of the science
units.arabic_anchors: «(وموضوعه المعلوم من حيث يتعلق بذلك)».
units.english: “Its subject is **the known**, insofar as it is connected with that”—that is, with the establishment of religious doctrines. The restriction “insofar as” is doing essential work: kalām is not simply an inventory of all knowable things, but a study of things under the regard in which they enter demonstrations concerning belief.
units.proof_note: Upper lemma and concise sharḥ, joined to I:12.

units.title: The author's use of ‘connection’
units.arabic_anchors: «(قوله أي بالعقائد الدينية الخ)» · «الأحكام والنسب» · «لا يتم بيان الموضوع بدون غير الموضوع».
units.english: The lower commentary objects that the phrase “insofar as it is connected with religious doctrines” requires explanation. The proof of a theological assertion may use not only doctrines but **relations, negations, and judgments** concerning items considered in other disciplines. Some things are not taken up because of their intrinsic nature, but because denying or affirming them makes a difference to an eventual conclusion. The author tests whether that consideration is sufficient to distinguish kalām from other sciences, or merely imports their questions wholesale.
units.proof_note: Connected lower source interpretation; incomplete literal transcript.

units.title: Predicates and the relation of the ‘known’
units.arabic_anchors: «(قوله المتناول للموجود والمعدوم)» · «المعلوم» · «الموضوع» · «المحمول».
units.english: The breadth of the known object matters especially when a question concerns a thing **that cannot exist**. The impossible is still an object of conceptual judgment: one can affirm its impossibility without giving it external existence. The gloss turns from this to a logical objection. If the theological matter is **predicated** of a subject rather than itself functioning as the subject term, can the definition still say “the known” is the science's subject? The discussion prepares the solution on I:13, where the predicates of theological problems are explicitly mentioned.
units.proof_note: Source-facing partial translation of the long lower continuation; the opening should be checked together with I:11.

units.title: Does a subject have to be demonstrable in every proposition?
units.arabic_anchors: «(قوله لا تبحث الخ)» · «بموضوعية الموضوع» · «اه منه».
units.english: The marginal note tests the claim that inquiry must always be about the subject *as such*. It is enough in some cases to understand how the subject or a property of the subject figures in a chain of demonstration. The distinction is again a matter of how propositions are organised within the science, not a proof that the things considered are all actual existents.
units.proof_note: Middle ruled note, partial reading. A compact clause requires another image check.

units.title: The range of auxiliary questions
units.arabic_anchors: «أي بالعقائد الدينية» · «أحوال المانع من القدم والوحدة» · «أحوال الجسم والعرض والحدوث والتركيب» · «أحوال المحال والمعدومات».
units.english: The connection intended is to **religious doctrines**. The scope of inquiry therefore includes characteristics that exclude a body's beginninglessness or absolute unity, the properties of body and accident, origination and composition, and questions about substantiality, individuation and other categories. It also extends to **impossibilities** and **nonexistents**, so far as propositions about them are needed to establish the desired doctrines. The scope is not limited to propositions that themselves state an article of faith; the inquiry can examine premises and distinctions used to demonstrate such propositions.
units.proof_note: Upper passage connected translation, lexical refinements still pending.

units.title: A common subject broad enough for nonexistents
units.arabic_anchors: «فالمعلوم المتناول للموجود والمعدوم» · «وقد قيل المعلوم».
units.english: Consequently the “known” can be taken broadly enough to embrace **existent and nonexistent** alike. This is why the discipline's subject cannot simply be “body,” “existent substance,” or another restricted ontological genus. Whatever is needed as a subject of intellectual judgment under the specified theological relation can enter consideration.
units.proof_note: Upper final sentence joins I:13.

units.title: Is the 'known' an adequate general subject?
units.arabic_anchors: «من الذهني وغيره يساوي الموجود المعدوم في العموم» · «إنما يحتاج إليه عند من يجعل مباحث المعدوم والمحال من مسائل علم الكلام» · «أن المراد بالعقائد الدينية المحمولات».
units.english: The marginal writer begins by challenging how the ‘known’ is supposed to extend to what exists only in thought as well as to what exists outside thought. Making the known object of inquiry fully coextensive with existence and nonexistence may be broader than the argument warrants. The issue becomes pressing especially if one counts discussion of the nonexistent and the impossible among the questions of kalām. The writer therefore asks whether the alleged subject is being construed as the *subject term* of the propositions, their *predicates*, or the whole range of things to which theological demonstration must refer. He reports the suggestion that ‘religious doctrines’ denotes the predicates, but cautions that this may not settle the problem by itself.
units.proof_note: Lower-gloss source-facing exposition, not a complete literal rendering of every line.

units.title: Indirect propositions and intermediate bases
units.arabic_anchors: «من حيثية التعلق بالمحمول كما يتناول الموضوع» · «ليس هذا الإخراج من ورطة» · «قال المصنف» · «ليس تصوراً لموضوعه».
units.english: The text develops a difficulty in restricting the discipline to its directly professed conclusions. It is not enough simply to say that what enters a proof as a premise is itself a credal conclusion: a science often studies conditions of its own arguments without taking each such condition as its final object. A predicate may be introduced under the respect in which it relates to an ultimate doctrinal result, just as a subject can be. The commentator uses this to question whether the proposed escape from the difficulty is genuine, rather than a shift between two ways of describing the same material.
units.proof_note: Connected argumentative paraphrase; several compact expressions at the top of the lower stream remain uncertain.

units.title: ‘Ultimate’ and ‘proximate’ ends of the discipline
units.arabic_anchors: «(قوله الفوز بسعادة الدارين)» · «ذكروا أن الفائدة والغاية والمنفعة أمور لا تختلف إلا بالحيثية والاعتبار» · «بالأحكام الشرعية اعتقاداً حقاً» · «لا يؤدي إلى الفساد في الآخرة».
units.english: On “attaining felicity in the two abodes”: benefit, end, and utility are not always three distinct realities; they may describe one result under different **considerations**. The nearer end of kalām is to establish firmly and correctly the doctrines that belong to religion, removing uncertainty and error. Its more remote end is a right faith that prevents misdirection in this life and leads toward deliverance in the next. The marginal writer objects to confusing this final good with the particular cognitive act that defines the science; something may be sought through the science without thereby becoming the science's own formal subject.
units.proof_note: Lower text partly normalized in English; the precise wording of the final lines joins I:14.

units.title: Sufficiency of the subject-based distinction
units.arabic_anchors: «المعلوم المذكور لا يعتبر من المحمول» · «المقصود من ذلك تمييز العلم من سائر العلوم باعتبار الموضوع» · «والبيان المذكور كاف فيه» · «اه منه».
units.english: The ‘known’ that was mentioned is not itself treated here as one of the predicates. The purpose is to distinguish this science from other sciences **by reference to its subject**, and the explanation given is sufficient for that. Allowing the discussion also to range over predicates does not destroy the proposed distinction. [The closing «منه» denotes a source or speaker, but does not independently identify a named glossator.]
units.proof_note: Separately ruled text; source-located reading.

units.title: Predicates of theological questions
units.arabic_anchors: «من الحيثية المذكورة يتناول محمولات مسائله» · «العقائد الدينية» · «المحمولات ...» · «فلا إشكال».
units.english: Under the respect already specified, the expression also embraces the **predicates** in the propositions that constitute its questions. One may therefore say that the religious doctrines intended here are the things predicated within the discipline, and what serves as the means of reaching those doctrines. On that understanding, the objection—that not every matter investigated is itself one of the credal conclusions—does not arise. [The precise intervening formulation after *al-maḥmūlāt* is difficult in this impression; the paraphrase is explicitly provisional.]
units.proof_note: Source-facing, interpretative at one indistinct phrase; no independent second proof.

units.title: Benefit and ultimate end
units.arabic_anchors: «وفائدته أمور وغاية الكل الفوز بسعادة الدارين» · «وكان المصنف يرى أنه من العلوم التي غايتها أنفسها فاكتفى ببيان ...».
units.english: The discipline has several benefits, while their ultimate end is **attaining felicity in the two abodes**. The commentator suggests that the author regarded this as one of the sciences whose immediate aim is, in one respect, its own knowledge. That helps explain why he was satisfied with specifying the discipline itself rather than treating every benefit or remoter aim as its defining subject.
units.proof_note: Connected upper-text reading; final word of the last clause requires a high-resolution recheck.

units.title: The two possible senses of an end
units.arabic_anchors: «العلم غاية لنفسه» · «لا تكون غاية الغاية» · «أن الأمور التي غايتها الفوز لا الفوز نفسه».
units.english: The marginal writer asks what the earlier reference to the end intends. If knowing itself is the immediate aim, a further end such as felicity can only be called the ‘end of the end’ under a particular ordering of aims. Not every benefit produced by a discipline is part of its essence or immediate purpose. The criticism is directed against sliding between the **knowledge sought**, the **good achieved through possessing it**, and the **farther religious outcome** of such possession.
units.proof_note: Lower-register source-based reading, selected clauses; not all words diplomatically transcribed.

units.title: Does knowledge of one's existence require prior knowledge of knowledge?
units.arabic_anchors: «تصور العلم بديهي» · «لوجهين الأول أنه معلوم» · «اكتساب الماهوية» · «فحكم الوجدان» · «إما ضرورة ... أو اكتساب».
units.english: The margin distinguishes knowing that one exists from possessing a definition of what ‘knowledge’ means. One may immediately have a cognition without being able to analyse its nature. The fact that something is given in awareness is not in itself a proof that its **quiddity**, as an object of reflective analysis, is also immediately apprehended. If one says that the conception of knowledge is acquired, a question remains: what knowledge must be present for the acquisition to take place? The argument is delicate because it can use *knowledge* for the act of apprehension in one premise and for the concept being studied in another.
units.proof_note: Partly interpretative lower reading; this distinction is explicit in the print, but the full argument is lengthy.

units.title: Circularity, ‘beginning’ and the limits of the proof
units.arabic_anchors: «يلزم الدور» · «بداهته مستلزمة لعدم تجدد» · «مستلزم للمطلوب المذكور» · «معلوم لا بالضرورة بل بالاكتساب».
units.english: The critic tests the regress argument by distinguishing an unqualified prior act of knowing from a reflexive act in which knowledge becomes its own object. If every act of knowing presupposed a previously **defined** notion of knowledge, a circle would indeed appear; but if an initial act can occur without reflective grasp of its nature, the inference requires another premise. Conversely, declaring that all cognition must be obtained through acquisition raises the question of its beginning. The marginal discussion does not treat these alternatives as automatically equivalent.
units.proof_note: Close source-guided synthesis. The sentence continues onto I:15.

units.title: A further end and the inadequacy of a strict definition
units.arabic_anchors: «فيكون هذا كذا غاية الغاية» · «والعلم لا حدّ له بوجهه» · «واختاره الإمام الرازي لوجهين».
units.english: In that case, this is the **end of the end**: a remoter result beyond the more immediate purpose of the science. The discussion then turns to *knowledge*. One position holds that it cannot be defined by a strict essential definition and instead must be made known in another way. The commentator reports that Imām Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī preferred this view and adduces two arguments for it.
units.proof_note: Upper text, first-pass connected translation.

units.title: Two arguments for immediacy
units.arabic_anchors: «الأول أن علم كل أحد بأنه موجود ضروري» · «وهذا أعم خاص والمطلق جزء منه» · «والثاني أن غير العلم يعلم بالعلم فلو علم العلم بغير العلم لزم الدور».
units.english: First, everyone’s knowledge that **he himself exists** is necessary or immediate; this is a determinate case of knowing, and knowledge considered without that determination is more general. It is argued that, if the particular is immediate, then the more general conception should be no less so. Second, other things are known **by means of knowledge**; if knowledge itself could be known only by way of a further act of knowledge, a vicious circle or regress appears to threaten. The text specifies that the second objection bears against one who says that knowledge is known but **not** necessarily or immediately.
units.proof_note: Upper text close reading. The inferential move from particular to general is an **argument being reported**, not endorsed by the editor.

units.title: Knowledge as an actuality of the knower
units.arabic_anchors: «حصول العلم» · «الضروري ... حصول علم جزئي بوجوده وهو غير تصوره» · «لم يصح وجهها إلا على عدم التحديد فقط».
units.english: The marginal commentator explains that the occurrence of a particular knowledge is not the same as an explicit, reflexive conception of the nature of knowledge. A person can be aware of his existence without arranging a definition of cognition. If one uses such awareness to argue that knowledge resists **essential definition**, that is a more modest conclusion than showing that no explanatory account of knowledge can be given. The second proposition needs a separate proof.
units.proof_note: Source-facing lower reading, not a literal complete mapping.

units.title: Whether self-consciousness is unavoidable
units.arabic_anchors: «أن حصول العلم العلم لا يعني حصول النفس إلى الذي وحصوله فيها» · «يكون حصوله في النفس تصوراً وحكاية» · «بالدليل الثاني».
units.english: The margin considers whether every occurrence of a cognitive state includes awareness of that occurrence. It distinguishes the presence of the knowing **act** in the soul from a subsequent representation or conception **of that act**. If the two are identified, the claim that self-awareness is necessary may appear plausible; if distinguished, the claim needs qualification. The discussion leads to the second proposed route for making knowledge understood, namely division and example rather than a strict definition.
units.proof_note: Several tightly printed clauses are insecure, especially the lead-in to I:16; the Arabic anchor is deliberately fragmentary.

units.title: Conception of the acquired cognition
units.arabic_anchors: «(قوله وهو غير تصوره)» · «لكن تصوره لازم لحصوله كما في سائر الوجدانيات» · «اه منه».
units.english: On “and it is not its conception”: nevertheless, one might contend that some conception is required for its occurrence, as with other objects of inner experience. Thus the distinction, while real, does not by itself establish that the cognition can occur without any accompanying apprehension of what is taking place. [Closing annotation has no positively established personal author.]
units.proof_note: Short separately ruled note, provisional source reading.

units.title: Resolving the first argument's equivocation
units.arabic_anchors: «على عدم التفرقة بين تصور العلم وحصوله» · «والضروري حصول علم جزئي بوجوده» · «وهو غير تصوره وغير العلم».
units.english: The objection rests on a **failure to distinguish between conceiving knowledge and its occurrence**. What is necessary here is the occurrence of a particular cognition of one’s own existence. That cognition's occurrence is not the same as the conception of the cognition, still less a universal definition of knowledge. Hence the first argument cannot simply carry the immediacy of one cognitive event over to the concept of knowledge as such.
units.proof_note: Upper text connected translation, with opening join from I:14.

units.title: The objection from acquired conceptions
units.arabic_anchors: «أما ... حصول علم جزئي ... يتوقف تصوره على تصوره» · «وقيل لا يجدي ...» · «وإليه ذهب الغزالي».
units.english: If the concept of knowledge is acquired, it is argued that some prior grasp of what one is acquiring may be required. Yet that cannot be established merely from the fact that a particular act of knowing has occurred. The discussion reports a further objection to the proposed distinction and associates a position in this dispute with al-Ghazālī. The crucial point is whether what requires a prior conception is **the acquired representation of knowledge**, or every instance of knowledge occurring in a knower.
units.proof_note: Upper passage partly compressed; attribution and precise final words should be rechecked before citation.

units.title: Is the knowledge of a division itself known through knowledge?
units.arabic_anchors: «وحصول العلم به يستلزم إمكان العلم بأنه عالم» · «فيلزم حصول العلم بالعلم الخاص قبل حصول العلم بمطلق العلم» · «مفهوماً مطلق العلم».
units.english: The lower commentator contests the logic of the proposed division. Knowing by an act may permit one to know that one is a knower, but this does not mean the **unrestricted concept of knowledge** must have been defined before the particular act occurred. Conversely, if the mind has to grasp the general category before any example becomes intelligible, the explanatory procedure may tacitly presuppose what it was intended to provide. The point hinges on keeping distinct a concrete cognitive act, reflective awareness of that act, and the general concept of knowledge.
units.proof_note: Connected reading of a major lower-register objection; unverified compressed subclauses remain.

units.title: The particular and the general
units.arabic_anchors: «حصول العلم بالعلم الخاص» · «حصول العلم بالعلم الغير» · «مطلق العلم» · «ليس فقط».
units.english: The marginal reasoning also asks how an item can be recognised as a **particular kind of knowledge** without prior conception of the general description. The author considers the contrary order as well: one might have a specific cognition and acquire a generic concept through subsequent comparison or reflection. That opposition is not resolved by simply calling either a particular or a general concept ‘necessary’; the alleged priority must itself be clarified.
units.proof_note: Source-facing exposition, not all lower lines supplied in literal English; the final marginal clause continues to I:17.

units.title: Why an example is not a definition
units.arabic_anchors: «(قوله وأما المثال)» · «يطلق على المشابه وعلى الجزئي» · «فالأول ... والثاني ...».
units.english: On “as for the example”: *mithāl* can refer to something **similar** or to a **particular instance**. The text assigns the two examples their different roles accordingly. An illustrative instance can make a state recognisable without supplying the essential features demanded of a strict definition.
units.proof_note: Short ruled note, first visual reading; precise ending requires recheck.

units.title: Four divisions of assent
units.arabic_anchors: «بالدليل الثاني وطريق معرفته عنده القسمة والمثال» · «الاعتقاد إما جازم أو غير جازم» · «والجازم إما مطابق للواقع أو غير مطابق» · «والمطابق إما ثابت أو غير ثابت».
units.english: The second route consists in making knowledge known through **division and example**. Under division: an assent is either firm or not firm; a firm assent is either in accordance with reality or not; and an assent in accordance with reality is either stable or unstable. In this way, one distinguishes certain knowledge from mere non-firm opinion, firm error, and even a correct belief that is not settled or secure. The divisions are supplied **to identify** knowledge, not as a strict definition giving its genus and essential differentia.
units.proof_note: Upper source text; each ternary split visually checked.

units.title: Example and the limits of an essential definition
units.arabic_anchors: «وأما المثال فكأن يقال العلم إدراك البصيرة» · «كاعتقادنا أن الواحد نصف الاثنين» · «لا يحدّ بعبارة جامعة للجنس والفصل الذاتي» · «والإحساس به معروف».
units.english: Under example, one might speak of knowledge as the insight of the inner faculty, or point to our certain conviction that **one is half of two**. The intention of the thinker cited is not that the word can never be explained, but that a definition collecting an essential genus and difference is difficult or impossible in the present case. Many things are recognised perfectly well through experience or example without an analysis that displays their ultimate essence. The example helps a reader identify the intended state even where a genus-and-difference definition cannot be supplied.
units.proof_note: Upper source-facing reading; punctuation and the exact phrase concerning insight need verification against a second impression.
